description: Tier-1 development diagnostic set derived from public RFC 8259 text. It is not sealed, externally authored, or a promotion benchmark.
purpose: Diagnose retrieval and grounded-answer failure modes across explicit public-source question types.

authoring_origin.basis: Questions, references, and labels were prepared from the cited RFC sections and the recorded 1000-character/200-overlap split.

answer_policy: Answer the question under one fixed policy. Use and cite retrieved contexts when supplied; without retrieved contexts, state that no retrieved evidence was supplied. If RFC 8259 does not specify the requested value, explicitly abstain from inventing one.
citation_policy: With retrieval enabled, cite supporting passages inline as [context:N]. RAG-off answers must not invent retrieved citations.

test_cases.query: Are TRUE, FALSE, and NULL valid JSON literal spellings under RFC 8259?
test_cases.reference_answer: No. The three literal names are true, false, and null, and they must be lowercase.

test_cases.query: Why are repeated member names in a JSON object a portability problem, and how may receivers differ?
test_cases.reference_answer: RFC 8259 says object names should be unique. With duplicates, receiver behavior is unpredictable: implementations may keep only the last pair, report an error or fail to parse, or expose all pairs.

test_cases.query: For JSON exchanged between independent systems, combine the RFC's encoding requirement with the parser's minimum acceptance obligation.
test_cases.reference_answer: Such JSON text must use UTF-8, and a JSON parser must accept every text that conforms to the JSON grammar; it may also accept extensions.

test_cases.query: What exact maximum JSON text size in bytes does RFC 8259 require every parser to accept?
test_cases.reference_answer: RFC 8259 does not prescribe a fixed byte maximum. It says an implementation may set a limit on the size of texts it accepts.

test_cases.query: Should a member name containing a reverse solidus compare equal when one spelling uses \u005C and the other uses the short escape? Explain the interoperable comparison method.
test_cases.reference_answer: Yes. Both spellings represent the same reverse solidus. Interoperable implementations convert textual spellings to Unicode code units and compare those units numerically; comparing unconverted escape text can give a false inequality.

test_cases.query: State one interoperability condition for object members and one type-related rule for array elements in RFC 8259.
test_cases.reference_answer: Object member names should be unique for interoperable name-value mappings. Array elements are not required to have the same type.

test_cases.query: How is a JSON exponent formed, and within what integer interval do binary64-based implementations agree exactly?
test_cases.reference_answer: An exponent starts with E or e, may include a plus or minus sign, and must then contain one or more digits. Binary64-based implementations agree exactly for integers from -(2^53)+1 through (2^53)-1.

test_cases.query: What can happen when JSON contains an unpaired UTF-16 surrogate such as \uDEAD?
test_cases.reference_answer: Receiver behavior is unpredictable. Implementations may disagree about string length or even suffer fatal runtime exceptions.

test_cases.query: Why does RFC 8259 reject using eval-like functions as a general JSON parser?
test_cases.reference_answer: It is generally an unacceptable security risk because input can contain executable code alongside data declarations; JSON and the host language syntax are also not identical in every case.

test_cases.query: Contrast the conformance obligations RFC 8259 places on a JSON parser and on a JSON generator.
test_cases.reference_answer: A parser must accept every text conforming to the JSON grammar and may accept extensions. A generator's output must strictly conform to the JSON grammar.
